q.t: The main test for a chemical change is…
q.e: Chemical change means one or more new substances form. That's the whole test.

q.t: Melting ice is a…
q.e: Ice becomes water — still the same substance, just a different state. No new substance.

q.t: Curdling of milk is a…
q.e: Curd is a new substance with different taste and properties, so it is chemical.

q.t: Folding a sheet of paper is a…
q.e: Only the shape changes; it is still paper.

q.t: Lime water turns milky with…
q.e: Carbon dioxide reacts with lime water to form white calcium carbonate — the standard CO₂ test.

q.t: Burning of a substance in oxygen giving heat and light is…
q.e: Combustion is a reaction with oxygen that releases heat and/or light.

q.t: The lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire is its…
q.e: Below its ignition temperature a fuel won't catch fire, even with oxygen around.

q.t: Which is NOT one of the three things a fire needs?
q.e: The fire triangle is fuel, oxygen and heat. Water is used to put fires out.

q.t: Ripening of fruit is a…
q.e: New substances (sugars, flavours) form, and we want it to happen.

q.t: Rusting of iron is a…
q.e: Rust is a new substance (iron oxide), so rusting is chemical — and unwanted.

q.t: Crushing chalk into powder cannot be undone. What kind of change is it?
q.e: It's still chalk, just smaller pieces. Being irreversible doesn't make a change chemical.

q.t: What is the white substance that makes lime water milky?
q.e: Calcium hydroxide + carbon dioxide → calcium carbonate + water. Calcium carbonate doesn't dissolve, so the water looks milky.

q.t: Vinegar and baking soda fizz. The gas turns lime water milky. The gas is…
q.e: Only carbon dioxide turns lime water milky.

q.t: A candle under a glass tumbler goes out after a while. Which part of the fire triangle was removed?
q.e: The trapped air's oxygen gets used up, and no fresh air can come in.

q.t: If someone's clothes catch fire, why wrap them in a thick blanket?
q.e: Without oxygen, the fire triangle breaks and the fire dies.

q.t: Why should the blanket NOT be synthetic?
o: It can melt and stick to the skin
It lets in too much air
q.e: Synthetic fibres melt with heat and can stick to the skin, causing worse burns.

q.t: In a burning candle, melting of wax is ___ and burning of wax vapour is ___.
q.e: Melting only changes state. Burning makes new substances like carbon dioxide and water.

q.t: Breaking of rocks in place by heat, cold, roots and water is called…
q.e: Weathering breaks rock down where it is. Erosion is moving the pieces away.

q.t: Carrying away of broken rock and soil by wind and water is called…
q.e: Erosion carries the pieces away. 'Weathering breaks it, erosion carries it.'

q.t: Fireflies make light without heat. This is called…
q.e: Bioluminescence is light made by a chemical change in living things, with very little heat.

q.t: Paper doesn't burn in sunlight, but burns under a magnifying glass. Which leg of the fire triangle did the glass supply?
q.e: Fuel (paper) and oxygen (air) were already there. Focused sunlight raised the paper past its ignition temperature.

q.t: Blowing into tap water through a straw only makes bubbles. Why is this a physical change?
q.e: The water stays clear; nothing new is made.

q.t: Which is an undesirable change?
q.e: Spoiled food is unwanted. The others are things we deliberately do.

q.t: Decomposing food waste into compost is…
q.e: The same decay that spoils stored food is useful in a compost pit. Whether a change is desirable depends on the situation.

q.t: Basalt rock gets a red layer over time. This is…
o: Chemical weathering — iron forms iron oxide
q.e: Iron in the rock reacts with air and water to form red iron oxide — a new substance, so it's chemical.

q.t: Water freezing in rock cracks splits the rock. This is…
q.e: Ice takes up more room than water and pushes the crack apart. The rock is still the same material.

q.t: Why are river pebbles smooth and round?
o: Erosion by flowing water rubs them
q.e: As water carries them, they knock and rub against each other — erosion wears off the sharp edges.

q.t: A lit matchstick sets paper on fire instantly because…
o: It is hotter than paper's ignition temperature
q.e: The flame heats the paper beyond its ignition temperature in an instant.

q.t: Which is a reversible change?
q.e: Melted wax can solidify again. The others can't be undone.

q.t: Magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide + heat + light. This reaction is…
q.e: Magnesium reacts with oxygen to form a new substance, giving heat and light — that is combustion.

q.t: Ice melting and chalk crushing are both physical. One is reversible, one isn't. What does this show?
o: Reversibility is a separate question from physical/chemical
q.e: Use 'is a new substance formed?' to sort physical/chemical. 'Can it be undone?' is a different question.

q.t: Lime water in a dish under a burning candle and tumbler turns milky. What does this prove?
q.e: Lime water turns milky only with CO₂. The carbon in the wax combined with oxygen in the air to make it.

q.t: A forest fire is stopped by cutting a wide strip of trees ahead of it. Which leg of the triangle is removed?
q.e: With no trees to burn in the strip, the fire runs out of fuel.

q.t: Water is thrown on burning wood. Mainly, which leg is attacked?
o: Heat — it cools below ignition temperature
q.e: Water absorbs heat and cools the wood below its ignition temperature (it also blocks some air).

q.t: Which pair is BOTH a chemical change?
q.e: Rust and cooked food are both new substances. The other pairs only change shape or state.

q.t: Sediment from erosion settles in the sea and hardens over thousands of years into…
q.e: Layers of sediment slowly harden into new rock — this cannot be reversed.

q.t: Why did Faraday think a candle was perfect for teaching science?
o: Melting, vaporising and burning all happen in one flame
q.e: A single candle shows physical changes (melting, evaporation) and a chemical change (burning) together.

q.t: A student says 'combustion always makes a flame'. Which example disagrees?
o: Paper charring under a magnifying glass before it flames
q.e: Combustion releases heat and/or light. Paper can smoulder and char before any flame appears.

q.t: Which test would you do to show a gas is carbon dioxide?
q.e: If lime water turns milky, the gas is carbon dioxide.

q.t: Sun-dried mud cracking and wind blowing away the dust are, in order…
q.e: First the soil/rock breaks up in place (weathering), then wind carries it away (erosion).
